question: Following Sony’s announcement that it intends to phase out physical games for new console releases starting in 2028, concerns about consumer rights have intensified. While Commissioner McGrath noted that the EU cannot compel private companies to produce physical goods, the full transition to closed digital ecosystems exposes consumers to single-vendor pricing dynamics, while also raising questions about non-transferable digital licences and possible loss of access to paid content. In this context: 1.

As this restriction of console ecosystems means that players and third-party developers are forced to face a single commercial gatekeeper, does the Commission intend to review and expand the scope of the Digital Markets Act to include dedicated video game console environments?

Is the Commission available to assess legislative initiatives that ensure consumers have irrevocable access to purchased video games, so as to prevent the loss of content upon, for example, server shutdowns, address misleading commercial terms like ‘Buy’ buttons for temporary licences, and safeguard the option for consumers to temporarily lend their acquired digital games?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.11.2026) The Digital Markets Act1 (DMA) only applies to a closed list of ten core platform services listed in Article 2(2) of the DMA (such as online search engines, social networking services, intermediation services, etc.) to the extent that they are provided by companies fulfilling the criteria to be designated as gatekeepers under the DMA.

As Sony is not currently designated as a gatekeeper, it is not subject to the DMA obligations. The Commission recently indicated2 that it does not envisage new legislation requiring continuous consumer access to video games and explained the reasons, notably, the existing EU rules protecting consumers and the providers’ intellectual property rights.

Existing EU consumer legislation3 indeed protects consumers in all the supply modes of digital content and services; these must always be in conformity with the contractual stipulations and the consumer’s reasonable expectations, including as regards their continuity. Digital providers must also provide consumers with clear information before the conclusion of the contract4.

Misleading commercial claims are prohibited when they cause average consumers to take transactional decisions that they would not have taken otherwise5. These EU instruments are transposed into national laws. Member States’ authorities and courts deal with their enforcement.

The mentioned possibility for consumers to lend their acquired video games is subject to the general requirements on conformity with the contract. In assessing the latter, also the rights of digital creators have to be taken into account since they hold copyright in their works and grant the right to use their works via licensing.
1 Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and the Council of 14 September 2022 on contestable

and fair markets in the digital sector and amending Directives (EU) 2019/1937 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Digital Markets Act). 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/C/2026/3601/oj/eng. 3 In particular, Directive (EU) 2019/770 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 May 2019 on certain aspects concerning contracts for the supply of digital content and digital services.

4 Directive 2011/83/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 October 2011 on consumer rights, amending Council Directive 93/13/EEC and Directive 1999/44/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and repealing Council Directive 85/577/EEC and Directive 97/7/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council.

5 Directive 2005/29/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 May 2005 concerning unfair business-to-consumer commercial practices in the internal market and amending Council Directive 84/450/EEC, Directives 97/7/EC, 98/27/EC and 2002/65/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council and Regulation (EC) No 2006/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council (‘Unfair Commercial Practices Directive’).
